I don't have any inside information to comment on this, but it's possible that Mark sees in [Alex](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexandr_Wang) kind of a potential successor to himself, like a younger version of himself.

#### The biggest misconception: zero technical contribution to Llama

**Jacob Effron:** Yeah, I feel like a lot of the popular narrative in the media has been like, oh, like, you know, when Alex comes in, it then gets harder to run a research organization. I don't know if to the extent you felt that, or —

**Yann LeCun:** Well, okay. So here's a big misconception about my role, my relation to Alex, and how AI was run at Meta. I had zero technical contribution to Llama. Like, none whatsoever.

My one contribution to Llama was to argue for open-sourcing Llama 2, because there was a big internal debate whether we should open-source. The legal department was against it, the policy department was kind of against it, the comms department was for it, all the engineering side was for it — like Boz was for it.

So there was enormous internal discussions at a very high level — 40 people from Mark Zuckerberg down, every week for two hours, for months. So really it was a big debate internally.

And I really, really, really argued for the fact that — and Boz also was very vocal about it — that the safety risks were basically overblown. The opportunities to create an industry were extremely strong. And that we were going to jumpstart the AI industry by open-sourcing Llama 2. And in fact that's exactly what happened.

So I had zero contribution to Llama, positive or negative. Like, I didn't do anything to stop it or slow it down or anything. There was a lot of people working on LLMs within FAIR and it was fine. I never said anything against it — other than saying, this is not a path to human intelligence, but it's fine. It's useful. Same thing for speech recognition, translation, right?

And particularly since 2018, when I stepped down from being director of FAIR, I didn't have any direct influence on what people were working on, other than basically publishing my vision and then rallying people around my project. But they were working with me because they wanted to, not because I was their boss. I wasn't telling them to work with me.

So I had no positive or negative influence on LLMs within Meta. And I had some influence on the strategy, but it was more like the long term and how you maintain a research lab and things like this.

And in the last year — starting maybe early 2024, and certainly in 2025 — the direction in which FAIR was being moved and managed basically did not correspond to what I thought was necessary to preserve innovation, research and breakthrough, and preserve the good people. Like, a lot of good people have left already.

**Jacob Effron:** Yeah. And I guess a lot of, you know, you probably was harder to get people to work on the stuff you were working on internally. And I'm sure there was pressure for you yourself to work on a lot of the LLM stuff.

**Yann LeCun:** Yeah, no, but a lot of other people also have left, right?

**Jacob Effron:** No, it's fascinating.

### [1:12:11 — Advice for PhD Students](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ngBraLDqzdI&t=4331s) {#ch-phd-advice}

#### What changed: self-supervised learning succeeded — for language, not video

**Jacob Effron:** I mean, one thing I'm struck by throughout our whole conversation is, I feel like you've had a remarkably consistent point of view in the space for a long time. And you can go back to a bunch of the earlier talks you referenced. Obviously it is a fast-moving space, and a ton of interesting things have happened in the last year. What's like one thing you've changed your mind on in the last year?

**Yann LeCun:** I mean, the whole idea of what we used to call unsupervised learning that we now call self-supervised learning. Until about 2003, the whole idea of unsupervised pre-training, where you get a good representation for the input data and then you either fine-tune the model with a little bit of supervised label data — and it sort of gives us some evidence that this whole technique could work.

I tried to apply this to video, because ultimately what I wanted to do is train a system to understand how the world works by just watching the world go by. Yeah. Right? I mean, that's the basic idea.

I sort of started to argue for this in the early 2010s. Did some work on simple video prediction. We didn't have GPUs.

And then sort of doing this more seriously after the creation of FAIR, by doing pixel-level video prediction, realizing that wasn't working, but then arguing for self-supervised learning.

Okay, this whole idea of training a system generically not to solve a task, but to basically just predict, and then using the representation that is learned this way as input to a downstream task that you can train supervised or reinforcement or whatever.

So that was a bit of the topic of my second half of my keynote at NeurIPS in 2016. It was still called NIPS at the time.

**Jacob Effron:** Yeah, of course.

**Yann LeCun:** In 2016. And then I kept pushing for this idea, and tried to discover some methods to get that to work. And what surprised me is that that became incredibly successful — but not for video. For language. LLMs basically are a blindingly successful example of self-supervised learning.

**Jacob Effron:** No, that they are.

#### The closing technical lecture: why representation collapse is the JEPA problem

Well, I feel that's almost like the perfect note to end on, but I want to make sure to leave the last word to you. I feel like all our listeners are very familiar with you, but I want to at least give you the mic to point them to anything that you think they should check out with some of the new stuff you're doing, or any of your work you want to point to. The mic is yours.

**Yann LeCun:** Okay. Let me tell you one thing. An LLM works because when you have a sequence of discrete symbols, making predictions is easy — because there's only a finite number of possible symbols in your language, 100,000 possible tokens or something like that, right?

And you can have your neural net produce a probability distribution over all possible tokens. And then you can sample from that distribution, shift the token into the input, and then produce the next token, and you can do [autoregressive prediction](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autoregressive_model). Okay, so that's a special case.

If you have the real world, you can't use a generative model. So now you have to train a system that learns a representation and makes predictions in the representation space.

There's a big issue with this — which I didn't think until about five years ago was easily solvable, even though I invented one technique to solve it decades before that. And it's the problem that, if you take two inputs — let's say the initial segment of a video and the continuation of that video, or you take one image and a corrupted version of it — you run them both through an encoder, and you train a predictor to predict the representation of one from the representation of the other, there's a very simple solution where the system basically predicts a constant representation.

In other words, the prediction problem becomes trivial. That's called a collapse — representation collapse.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** A useful intuition for why this is JEPA's defining problem: the JEPA training signal measures *agreement* between two encoded representations, not their *content*. Concretely, take two related inputs (e.g., a video frame $x_t$ and a future frame $x_{t+k}$). Pass each through the encoder: $z_t = E(x_t)$, $z_{t+k} = E(x_{t+k})$. Train a predictor $P$ to map $z_t \to \hat{z}_{t+k}$. The loss is $\| P(z_t) - z_{t+k} \|^2$.

Now suppose the encoder degenerates so that $E(x) = c$ — the same constant vector — for every input. Then $z_t = c$ and $z_{t+k} = c$ for any pair of frames. The predictor is only ever queried at one input, $c$, so its output is some fixed vector $p = P(c)$ — whatever it happens to be. Gradient descent then jointly drives $c$ and $p$ to coincide, and the loss $\|p - c\|^2$ reaches zero. **Perfect minimization, zero learning.** The two representations agree because the entire encoder-predictor pair has collapsed to a trivial fixed point, not because the model has discovered anything about the inputs.

Generative models (autoregressive LLMs, VAEs, diffusion) don't have this failure mode because they have to *reconstruct* the input from the representation, which anchors it — a constant encoder would make every input's reconstruction the same, blowing up the loss. JEPA has no reconstruction term; only the consistency signal, which the trivial solution kills perfectly.

Concretely, a collapsed encoder is downstream-useless — every input maps to $c$, so the model can't distinguish anything. The three fix families [LeCun describes next](#ch-phd-advice) each kill the trivial fixed point in a different way: contrastive methods force pairs of different inputs apart with explicit negative samples; distillation/EMA methods (BYOL [[15]](#ref-15), DINO [[5]](#ref-5)) break the symmetric gradient path that would otherwise drive both encoders to a constant; and information-content regularizers (VICReg [[18]](#ref-18), SIGReg [[17]](#ref-17)) directly penalize low-entropy representations.
:::

So the big question of self-supervised learning for JEPA, for the joint-embedding architecture, is: how do you prevent collapse?

#### Three families of fixes: contrastive, distillation, and regularizer methods

**Jacob Effron:** Yeah.

**Yann LeCun:** The solution that I came up with many years ago — 1993 — is [contrastive learning](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Contrastive_learning) [[12]](#ref-12). So basically you have examples of things that should be predictable from one another, and an example of things that should not be predictable from one another. It turns out this method works, but it doesn't scale with dimension. It doesn't scale very well.

There's another technique that was actually invented by [Geoff Hinton](https://www.cs.toronto.edu/~hinton/) and [Suzanna Becker](https://psychology.mcmaster.ca/people/becker.html) in the late 80s — late 80s, I'm sorry — where you have those two networks and you try to maximize the [mutual information](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mutual_information) between them [[13]](#ref-13).

[Jürgen](https://people.idsia.ch/~juergen/) is mad at me, because he also came up with a version of this in 1992 [[14]](#ref-14), and he says that's JEPA. It's not JEPA. It's just another way of preventing collapse of a joint-embedding architecture. Which is fine, but it's not, you know, it's a particular way of doing it, which I don't think is particularly good.

Okay. So now you have this JEPA architecture. You have to come up with a good way of preventing collapse, and there is a couple ways. So as I already said, contrastive methods I think is not a good approach. There's another set of methods that are kind of called distillation methods, and they do prevent collapse — we don't know why. So a good example of that is DINO.

**Jacob Effron:** Yeah.

**Yann LeCun:** That's a joint-embedding method using the distillation method. Basically, one of the encoders trains the other one, is used as a teacher for the other encoder. The encoder that is being trained, you do backprop to. The one that is not being trained, you don't do backprop, but you share the weights with the other one with some [exponential moving average](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Exponential_smoothing).

It's a collection of recipes. There's a paper from DeepMind about it called [Bootstrap Your Own Latent (BYOL)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.07733) [[15]](#ref-15), which uses this trick. That trick is derived from some intuition from reinforcement learning, and somehow it prevents collapse, but we don't know why. There are a few theoretical papers on it that explain why it possibly might work in some simple cases, but it's not satisfactory.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The two most-cited theoretical analyses of why BYOL avoids collapse without negative samples are [Tian, Chen, and Ganguli 2021](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.06810) [[20]](#ref-20) — which analyzes the eigenstructure of the predictor + stop-gradient combination under linear-network and isotropic-data assumptions — and [Wen and Li 2022](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.06226) [[21]](#ref-21), which characterizes the role of the prediction head specifically. Both confirm collapse is avoided in simplified settings, but neither closes the gap that LeCun flags here: the loss the optimizer actually descends isn't the loss you can monitor in training, so practitioners can't tell from the loss curve whether collapse is happening.
:::

The cost function you think you're minimizing — you're not actually minimizing. And so you can't monitor it. It actually goes up when you train. So we don't like this method, but it works.

And some of the models we've trained, large-scale video representation learning systems — V-JEPA, [V-JEPA 2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.09985) [[16]](#ref-16), V-JEPA 2.1 — they train using this method. JEPA also. But we're moving away from this.

#### The third family: information-content regularizers (VICReg, SIGReg) and LeWorldModel

And now we have a few papers that came out recently on an explicit regularizer to prevent this collapse, which basically tries to maximize the information content coming out of the encoder. So it's in the same family as the Becker and Hinton from '89 and the Schmidhuber 1992, and a bunch of others since then, and to some extent also contrastive techniques — although it's not sample-contrastive.

And then the question is, how do you measure information content? How do you maximize the information content coming out of a neural net?

The problem is, if you want to maximize the quantity, you either need to be able to measure it, or you need to have a lower bound on it.

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** The intuition behind the regularizer family: collapse is the limit case where the encoder outputs carry *zero* information about the input — every input maps to the same $c$, so the entropy of the representation distribution is zero. If you can force the encoder's output distribution to have high entropy — i.e., spread across the latent space rather than concentrated on a single point — collapse is mechanically excluded. No need for negative samples (contrastive) or asymmetric architectural tricks (BYOL/DINO); the regularizer term in the loss does the work directly.

The technical obstacle LeCun flags is that differential entropy of a continuous distribution isn't easy to estimate from samples — you can only construct *upper* bounds (estimators that overstate true entropy). Maximizing an upper bound isn't a guarantee, so practitioners maximize a tractable proxy and hope the bound is tight enough.

The two methods named here implement that proxy differently:

- **VICReg [[18]](#ref-18)** is three terms — **V**ariance (each feature dimension must have at least unit variance, so no dimension can collapse), **I**nvariance (paired views agree on their representations, the original JEPA consistency signal), and **C**ovariance (off-diagonal terms of the feature covariance matrix are pushed to zero, decorrelating features so they don't all encode the same information). Spread + decorrelate.
- **SIGReg [[17]](#ref-17)** is one term: project the encoder output onto many random 1-D directions and run a normality (Epps–Pulley) test on each projection. Aggregating the test statistics pushes the joint distribution toward an isotropic Gaussian. Why an isotropic Gaussian? Under fixed variance, the Gaussian distribution has *maximum* differential entropy — so matching that target is equivalent to maximizing information content under a unit-variance constraint. The LeJEPA paper [[17]](#ref-17) proves the isotropic Gaussian is the optimal target distribution for JEPAs.
:::

**Jacob Effron:** Yeah.

**Yann LeCun:** Information content, we only have upper bounds. We cannot measure it. We can only come up with upper bounds. And so we take an upper bound and we cross our fingers. Okay. And it kind of works.

So the latest one is called [SIGReg](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.08544) [[17]](#ref-17) — that means Sketched Isotropic Gaussian Regularization. We had a previous one called [VICReg](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.04906) [[18]](#ref-18) — variance-invariance-covariance regularization. And the SIGReg stuff is really cool.

This is some work by [Randall Balestriero](https://randallbalestriero.github.io/), who was a postdoc with me, is an assistant professor at [Brown University](https://www.brown.edu/) now. And it basically consists in forcing the distribution of variables coming out of the encoder to be jointly Gaussian, essentially — sort of maximize information, if you want, just a very different way of doing it than what Jürgen Schmidhuber and Suzanna Becker and Geoff Hinton were doing.

So this is super promising, in my opinion. And we have variations of it — one that can produce sparse representations, another one that can produce isotropic representations but not necessarily Gaussians.

And we have a paper with Randall — student at [Mila](https://mila.quebec/) — where we train a world model with this. It's still small scale, but I think it's super promising.

So if you want to read one paper, read that paper. It's [LeWorldModel](https://arxiv.org/abs/2603.19312) [[19]](#ref-19).

::: {.callout-note}
**Editor's note.** When LeCun says "a paper with Randall — student at Mila," he conflates two people. Randall Balestriero is the assistant prof at Brown; the student at Mila is [Lucas Maes](https://mila.quebec/en/directory/lucas-maes), lead author of LeWorldModel [[19]](#ref-19).
:::

**Jacob Effron:** Awesome. We'll definitely link to it too.

**Yann LeCun:** Yeah, I'm not responsible for the name. Randall picked it up.

**Jacob Effron:** Amazing. Well, Yann, seriously, thank you so much. It is such a privilege to get to spend the last bit of time with you, and really appreciate you coming on the podcast.

**Yann LeCun:** Thanks for having me. That was fun.

#### Outro: Jacob's signoff

**Jacob Effron:** I'm Jacob Effron, and this has been *Unsupervised Learning*, a podcast where I get to talk to the smartest people in AI and ask them tons of questions about what's happening with models and what it means for businesses in the world. As I hope is clear, I have a ton of fun doing this. It's a nights-and-weekends project in addition to my day job as an investor at [Redpoint](https://www.redpoint.com/).

But our ability to get these incredible guests on really comes from folks like you subscribing to the podcast, sharing it with friends. It's really what ultimately makes this whole thing work. And so please consider doing that. And thank you so much for your support and listening. We'll see —
